Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
I read the whole report. It is the most important document in the series, because it tests the claims the earlier papers left open. Most of its conclusions hold up:
- In the Varden case-processing offices, the per-hour gain shrank but did not disappear. That refutes the re-analysis's "entirely an artifact."
- The meta-analysis's "no sign of decay" rested on four uncontrolled studies that measured scheduled hours, which is a strong correction.

Four things need fixing:
- the definition of the system-log hours measure;
- contamination of the control group;
- the strength of the mediation claims;
- the Halden subset.

## Arithmetic check

These all reproduce:
- **Per-hour gains at 24 months:** 0.966 / 0.88 gives +9.8% on timesheets, and 0.966 / 0.89 gives +8.5% on system logs.
- **Mediation shares:** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100.
- **Halden continuers:** 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866, or −13.4%. Then 96.8 / 86.6 gives +11.8%.
- **Counter-arm staffing:** an 11.4% fall in output per employee implies about 13% more staff to restore it. That fits the 12% cited. A cost rise of 9% per contact (not 12%) would imply staff make up about three-quarters of costs. The report should state that assumption.

## Main issues

**1. The system-log hours measure contradicts the meeting data.**
The logs are described as recording "time staff are working on cases." If they really count only case work, then meetings fall outside them. Treated offices cut meetings by about 3.3 hours a week relative to control. Total hours fell by about 4.5 hours, so case-working time should have fallen by only about 1 hour, roughly 3–4%, not 11%.

There are two possibilities:
- **The logs record whole log-in sessions, meetings included.** Then they are a measure of total hours, and the description is wrong.
- **The logs record only case work.** Then the 11% fall conflicts with the meeting figures, and the mediation result needs rethinking. Cutting meetings can't raise output per hour of case work simply by removing non-case time. It could only work through something like less fragmented working days.

The report needs to state exactly what the logs count. That also affects how far log hours can "confirm" the timesheets.

**2. Two control offices changed their practice, which affects the decay estimate.**
At month 15, two of the seven control offices ran a "meeting audit" and saw about +4.1% output per hour. If that improvement was real, the control group's average rose by roughly 1.2 percentage points from month 15 onward. That would account for a large part of the fall from 12.5% to 9.8%.

So the decline may partly reflect the controls improving, not only the treatment effect fading. The report presents the observation only as a hint about reorganisation, but it is also a threat to the main decay estimate. The authors should:
- show the treated offices' own before-and-after trajectory separately from the comparison with control;
- re-estimate the effect with those two offices excluded or modelled separately, as a sensitivity check;
- ask whether the audits were prompted by hearing about the treated offices. If so, this is contamination between arms, not independent change.

The +4.1% figure itself compares the two offices only with their own previous six months. The other five control offices over the same months are a ready-made comparison and should be used.

**3. Decay is suggested, not demonstrated.**
The 9-month and 24-month confidence intervals overlap almost completely (+6.9 to +18.4 versus +4.6 to +15.2). The report gives no estimate or interval for the change between them. "Declined by about a quarter" compares two point estimates. The careful phrase "consistent with some fading" is right; the summary's flat "has therefore declined" goes further than the data. Combined with point 2, the true amount of fading is uncertain in both directions.

**4. The mediation analysis "supports" more than it "confirms".**
- **Number of clusters:** there are 14 offices. Counting "office-months" adds repeated measurements of the same offices, not independent data. An interval of 28–66% looks narrow for 14 clusters. The report should state how the clustering was handled, and whether the small-cluster corrections raised at nine months were applied. The same applies to every confidence interval in Table 1.
- **Assumptions:** mediation requires that nothing unmeasured drives both the mediators and the outcome. The limitations section admits this, but the summary still says "confirms."
- **Timing:** it isn't clear whether the meeting and fatigue measures come before the output they are meant to explain, or are measured at the same time.
- **Baseline meeting data:** the nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six. This report gives baseline figures of 7.4 and 7.2 hours. These were presumably reconstructed from calendar archives, and the report should say so. The near-equal baselines are reassuring, since they suggest randomisation balanced meeting time.

"Supported by a registered test" is accurate. "Confirms" is not.

**5. The Halden subset has more problems than the report acknowledges.**
- **Overlap with earlier reversions:** the original pilot already reported five reversions, three of them in retail and hospitality. Are the hospitality group and retail chain here among those five, or new reversions? The answer changes how the 24-month picture should be read.
- **The marketing agency:** it reverted over client deadlines. That is deadline-driven, discretionary work, not a coverage problem. It undercuts the clean coverage-versus-discretionary split, and the summary's "all with client-facing or coverage obligations" glosses over it.
- **"Upper bound":** the figure isn't guaranteed to be an upper bound. With no comparison group, two years of general productivity trends are included in the 11.8%, and those could push it either way.
- **Unexplained baseline match:** the baseline of 40.3 hours is identical to the re-analysis's 27-organisation time-tracking figure. The 17-organisation subset had 40.4. It may be a coincidence, but it's worth checking.
- **Non-response:** 9 of 23 organisations didn't respond, and their outcomes are unknown.
- **Conflict of interest:** R. Okafor is a co-author of the Halden pilot. The report should declare this. It should also respond to the re-analysis's finding that the pilot misreported when organisations withdrew, since a Halden author is now presenting Halden data.

**6. Some outcomes the nine-month report promised are missing.**
The nine-month report named backlog build-up beyond statutory deadlines as a key risk. At 24 months, the report should show:
- backlog size;
- age of cases;
- the share of cases closed within deadline.

Without these, steady case closures could hide a growing backlog or easier cases being picked first. The other secondary outcomes also need tests and intervals: the appeal-overturn rates (3.2% v 3.0%) and resignations (4.1% v 7.9%) have neither.

## Smaller points

- **Counter-arm stopping rule:** the arm was stopped on waiting times. The report should say whether that stopping rule was pre-specified. Either way, the decision is itself evidence: the county judged the service cost unacceptable.
- **"Log data show slightly more work":** this refers to changes relative to control, not levels. Spell that out.
- **Month-ten extrapolation:** rebutting "zero by month ten" is fair, but that extrapolation was weak to begin with. The data actually imply about month nine, and it was a straight line through two points. The stronger rebuttal is simply the 24-month estimate itself.
- **Separating reorganisation from the hours cut:** the closing question is the right one. A three-arm trial would answer it: reduced hours, reorganisation at full hours, and control. This is worth recommending explicitly.

## Where the five documents now stand

| Question | Best current answer |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain in discretionary work? | Real; about 8–10% on the best measures. The early pilot figures of over 20% were inflated. |
| Output per employee in discretionary work? | Roughly maintained, perhaps a few percent lower. |
| Coverage-bound work? | Output per employee falls about 9–11%. Service worsens unless staff are added, at about 9–12% higher cost. |
| Does the gain last? | Probably shrinks somewhat but persists to 24 months. The size of the fade is uncertain (control contamination, overlapping intervals). |
| Mechanism? | Fewer meetings probably explain a large share; fatigue a smaller one. This rests on one trial with 14 offices. |
| Could reorganisation alone capture it? | Unknown. No study has tested reorganisation without an hours cut. |

I can write this up as a short evidence summary, or draft a referee report on the follow-up.
